title: Inheritance and Interfaces
summary: Reuse and specialise behaviour with base classes, virtual and override, abstract classes, and define contracts with interfaces that unrelated classes can implement.
introduction: Inheritance lets a class take everything another class has and add or change behaviour; interfaces let completely different classes promise the same set of members. Together they make polymorphism possible: code written against a base type or an interface runs unchanged with any type that derives from or implements it. This lesson builds an animal hierarchy with virtual methods, an abstract Shape class, a notifier interface with two implementations, and shows how to test an object's type at runtime.
learningObjectives: Derive a class from a base class and override virtual members
Decide between an abstract class and an interface
Write code against a base type or interface so that new types work without changes

blocks.text: Writing `class Dog : Animal` makes `Dog` a **derived** class of the **base** class `Animal`: a `Dog` has every public and protected member of `Animal` and can be used wherever an `Animal` is expected. A base member marked `virtual` may be replaced in the derived class with `override`. A derived class's primary constructor passes along the arguments the base needs with `: Animal(name)`.

The loop variable has type `Animal`, yet `Speak()` runs the `Dog` and `Cat` versions. The runtime looks at the actual object, not the declared type: this is **polymorphism**. A derived class can still call the base version with `base.Speak()`, which is useful when you want to extend rather than replace behaviour. C# allows only one base class per class, and a class marked `sealed` cannot be derived from at all.

Sometimes the base class has no sensible implementation of its own: there is no such thing as the area of "a shape". Marking the class `abstract` forbids `new Shape()`, and an `abstract` member has no body and *must* be overridden. Abstract classes still provide shared state and concrete methods, such as `Describe` below, to every subclass.

blocks.text: An **interface** lists members without implementing them; a class that implements the interface promises to provide every one of them. Unlike base classes, a class may implement any number of interfaces, and unrelated classes can share one. Interface names start with `I` by convention. Code that depends on `INotifier` does not care whether a message goes by email or SMS, which makes it easy to add a third channel later or to substitute a fake in tests.

blocks.text: The base library is built on interfaces, and implementing them plugs your types into existing machinery. `IComparable<T>` lets `Sort` order your objects, `IEnumerable<T>` lets `foreach` and LINQ iterate them, and `IDisposable` lets `using` clean up resources. Implementing `IComparable<Player>` below is all it takes for `Array.Sort` to work.

When you hold a base type or `object`, the `is` operator tests the actual type and, with a **declaration pattern**, gives you a correctly typed variable in one step. The `as` operator converts or yields `null` instead of throwing, and a cast `(string)item` throws `InvalidCastException` when the type does not match.

blocks.text: Interfaces may also carry **default implementations** since C# 8, but that feature exists mainly for evolving public libraries; in everyday code keep interfaces as pure contracts. Many designs use both: an interface for the contract and an abstract base class that implements the boring parts.

blocks.title: Forgetting virtual or override
blocks.text: If the base method is not `virtual`, or the derived method lacks `override`, the derived method *hides* the base one instead of replacing it: calls through an `Animal` variable still run the base version, and the compiler warns with *CS0108: 'Dog.Speak()' hides inherited member 'Animal.Speak()'*. Mark the base method `virtual` and the derived one `override`; never silence the warning with `new` unless hiding is really what you want.

questions.question: Which of these can a C# class do?
questions.explanation: C# has single inheritance for classes but a class may implement any number of interfaces. Only virtual or abstract members can be overridden, and abstract classes cannot be instantiated.
options: Override a method that is not virtual
Be created with new while marked abstract

questions.question: To let a derived class replace a base-class method, the base method is marked `___` and the derived method is marked `override`.
questions.explanation: `virtual` opts a member in to being overridden; `abstract` does the same while leaving out the body.
